nameStory: The common onion gets its name from the Latin 'cepa,' which simply means onion - showing just how fundamental this bulb has been to human civilization for millennia. It's called 'common' because it's the most widely cultivated of all the onion species worldwide. The bulbous base that gives onions their characteristic shape comes from the plant storing energy in modified underground leaves that wrap around a central stem.
description: The common onion is a cultivated vegetable plant that's rarely found growing wild in New England, though it occasionally escapes gardens. It grows as a clump of hollow, bluish-green leaves that emerge from an underground bulb, reaching about 1-3 feet tall. The familiar papery-skinned bulb forms at the base when the plant reaches maturity, and in its second year, it may send up a tall flowering stalk with white or purple globe-shaped flower clusters. This is the same onion you'd find in your kitchen garden or grocery store.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Hollow, tube-like leaves that are bluish-green and feel smooth to the touch - pinch one and you'll feel the empty space inside, unlike solid grass blades

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Crush a leaf or scratch the bulb and you'll get that unmistakable sharp, pungent onion smell that might make your eyes water - no other New England plant smells quite like this

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in neat clumps or rows, usually near old garden sites or compost areas, with leaves emerging directly from the ground in a fan pattern

idTips.label: Bulb
idTips.description: Underground bulb with papery, brownish outer layers that you can peel away to reveal white or purple-tinged flesh beneath - feels firm and solid when squeezed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: In second year, produces a single tall, hollow flower stalk topped with a dense, round cluster of small white or light purple star-shaped flowers

habitat: Common onions are almost exclusively found near human habitation in New England - look for them in abandoned gardens, around old homesteads, near compost piles, or in disturbed soil where they've escaped cultivation. They prefer well-drained, fertile soil and full sun. You're most likely to spot them in suburban areas, old farmsteads, or along roadsides where garden waste has been dumped.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from bulbs, appearing as fresh green shoots poking through the soil. This is when the onion smell is strongest if you disturb the plants.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are fully developed and hollow, bluish-green tubes. Mature plants may send up tall flower stalks with globe-shaped white or purple flower clusters.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back, and the outer bulb layers become papery and dry. This is traditionally harvest time for the bulbs.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to underground bulbs, leaving little visible above ground except perhaps some dried stalks from the previous year's flowers.

funFact: Despite being one of humanity's oldest cultivated crops, the common onion has completely lost its ability to survive in the wild - scientists have never found its original wild ancestor, and it exists only because humans have been carefully tending it for over 7,000 years!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with wild garlic or wild leeks, but common onions have distinctly hollow leaves (pinch them to feel the tube), while wild garlic has solid, flat leaves and wild leeks have broader, solid leaves. The classic kitchen-onion smell when crushed is also a dead giveaway - it's much sharper and more familiar than its wild relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that the common onion is essentially a domesticated plant that can't survive without human care - unlike its wild cousins like ramps or wild garlic that thrive in New England forests. Any onions you find 'wild' are really just garden escapes trying to make it on their own.
compareHints: Common onions differ from their wild Allium relatives by having distinctly hollow, tubular leaves and that familiar sharp kitchen-onion scent. Wild leeks (ramps) have broad, flat, solid leaves that smell more garlicky, while wild garlic has narrow, solid, grass-like leaves. Chives have hollow leaves too, but they're much thinner and grow in dense clumps with purple pom-pom flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wide leek stands out from other wild onions by having broad, flat leaves instead of narrow, tubular ones.
Wild garlic differs from other Alliums by its completely hollow, tubular leaves - wild leeks have flat, broad leaves, while chives have thin but solid leaves.
Unlike their larger cousins wild leek (ramps) which have broad, flat leaves, or wild garlic with its flat, grass-like foliage, chives have distinctively round, hollow leaves that are much thinner.

Among New England Alliums, garlic chives are unique for their flat, strap-like leaves - wild garlic has narrow tubular leaves, ramps have broad oval leaves, and regular chives have hollow cylindrical leaves.
Canadian Meadow Garlic differs from its cousin Wild Leek (ramps) by having thin, grass-like leaves rather than broad, flat leaves, and it grows in sunny areas rather than shaded forests.
Among New England's wild onions, nodding onion is the only one with distinctively drooping flower heads—wild garlic and field garlic hold their flowers upright in tight, rounded clusters.
Unlike other New England Alliums such as wild garlic, chives, or wild leeks that produce typical flower clusters, Egyptian Walking Onion is unmistakable with its bulblet clusters.
Among its Allium relatives, garlic is distinguished by its segmented bulb structure — wild onions and leeks have single, solid bulbs rather than the characteristic cloves.
Yellow onion stands out from other New England Alliums by its bright golden-yellow flowers - most wild onions and garlics have white, pink, or purple blooms.
Ramsons stands out from other New England wild onions by having the broadest, flattest leaves in the genus - most other Alliums here have narrow, grass-like or tubular leaves.

Wild leek stands out from other New England Alliums by being much larger and more robust - while wild garlic and chives have thin, grass-like leaves, and ramps have broad leaves that disappear before flowering, wild leek maintains its broad, blue-green leaves right through the blooming period.
Field garlic differs from wild garlic by having flower heads that contain both actual flowers and bulblets mixed together, while wild garlic usually produces only bulblets.
Unlike New England's native wild onions such as wild leek or wild garlic which have narrow, grass-like green leaves, Turkistan onion stands out with its broad, silvery-blue foliage.

Small Yellow Onion stands out dramatically from other New England Alliums due to its bright yellow flowers - most of our native and naturalized onions like Wild Garlic, Nodding Onion, and Wild Leek have white, pink, or purplish flowers.

Unlike other wild Alliums in New England like wild garlic or ramps, honey garlic has uniquely drooping, bell-shaped flowers rather than the upright, star-shaped or rounded flower clusters typical of most onion relatives.
